title: Roadmap 2: language core (exceptions, functional style, memory, patterns)
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Checked versus unchecked exceptions and context managers, streams and generators, string immutability, memory management in the JVM and CPython, and common design patterns.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: A Java method you call is declared void load() throws IOException, and IOException is a checked exception. What must the caller do for the code to compile?

options.text: Catch IOException, or declare throws IOException (or a supertype) on the calling method.
options.why: Right: the compiler enforces handle-or-declare for checked exceptions.

options.text: Wrap the call in try-with-resources, which handles any exception for you.
options.why: try-with-resources closes resources but you still need a catch or a throws clause.

options.text: Nothing, because the compiler checks only RuntimeException subclasses.
options.why: It is the reverse: RuntimeException and Error are unchecked and exempt from the rule.

options.text: Mark the calling method final so the exception cannot propagate further.
options.why: final affects overriding, not exception flow.

questions.explanation: Checked exceptions model recoverable conditions the caller must acknowledge; unchecked ones signal programming errors. Spring favours unchecked exceptions, so wrap checked ones at the boundary.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about Python context managers and the with statement are true?

options.text: __exit__ runs even when the body of the with block raises an exception.
options.why: Right: that is why with is the safe way to close files and release locks.

options.text: A generator decorated with @contextlib.contextmanager can implement one using a single yield.
options.why: Right: code before yield is setup, code after it is teardown (use try/finally around yield).

options.text: If __exit__ returns a truthy value, the exception raised in the body is suppressed.
options.why: Right: returning False or None lets the exception propagate.

options.text: __exit__ runs only when the body completes without raising.
options.why: It always runs; the exception details are passed as its arguments.

options.text: with immediately deletes the object and frees its memory when the block ends.
options.why: It only calls __exit__; the object lives on until its refcount reaches zero.

questions.explanation: with is Python's try-with-resources. Interviewers like contextmanager examples such as timers, transactions and temporary directories.

questions.prompt: A text editor must support undo and redo for typing, deleting and formatting actions. Which design pattern fits best?

options.text: Command: each action is an object with execute() and undo(), kept on stacks.
options.why: Right: storing reversible command objects makes undo and redo a stack operation.

options.text: Observer: views subscribe to the document and are notified whenever any change happens.
options.why: Observer updates listeners, but does not capture how to reverse an action.

options.text: Singleton: one shared editor instance holds the current document text.
options.why: Singleton controls instance count, not reversible actions.

options.text: Factory: a creator method builds the right action object from user input.
options.why: A factory may create commands, but it provides no history or reversal itself.

questions.explanation: Command turns a request into an object, which also enables queueing, logging and macros. Strategy and Command look similar in code; Strategy swaps an algorithm, Command records an action.

options.text: A Map<String, List<String>> from each city to the names of the people in it.
options.why: Right: groupingBy keys by city and mapping converts each group to its list of names.

options.text: A Map<String, Long> from each city to the number of people who live in that city.
options.why: That would need Collectors.counting() as the downstream collector.

options.text: A List<String> of every distinct city found in the people stream.
options.why: groupingBy produces a Map, not a flat list.

options.text: A Map<String, Person> holding one arbitrary person per city.
options.why: That is toMap behaviour; groupingBy keeps all members of a group.

questions.explanation: The downstream collector decides what each group becomes: toList, counting, summingInt, mapping, and so on. Remember streams are lazy until a terminal operation and cannot be reused.

questions.prompt: The Python expression (x * x for x in range(10**9)) allocates the full list of one billion squares as soon as it is created.

options.text: True
options.why: A generator expression is lazy, so nothing is computed or stored until it is iterated.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: generator expressions produce values on demand, so memory stays constant; square brackets would build the list.

questions.explanation: Use generators and itertools (islice, chain, groupby) to stream large data. A generator is single-pass: once exhausted it yields nothing again.

questions.prompt: In Java, new String("a") == "a" evaluates to false even though new String("a").equals("a") is true.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: the literal "a" lives in the string pool, while new String creates a distinct heap object.

options.text: False
options.why: new always creates a new object, so the references differ; only equals compares the characters.

questions.explanation: Compare strings with equals, never ==. Strings are immutable, so repeated concatenation in loops creates many objects; use StringBuilder in Java and "".join(parts) in Python.

questions.prompt: In CPython, two objects reference only each other and nothing else references either. What reclaims them?

options.text: The cyclic garbage collector, since reference counts alone never reach zero.
options.why: Right: refcounting frees most objects at once, and the generational cycle collector handles cycles.

options.text: Reference counting alone, because every single count drops to zero right away.
options.why: Each object still holds a reference to the other, so neither count reaches zero.

options.text: Nothing; they leak until the interpreter process exits.
options.why: The cycle collector in the gc module finds and frees unreachable cycles.

options.text: The __slots__ declaration, which breaks references between objects.
options.why: __slots__ only removes the per-instance __dict__ to save memory.

questions.explanation: CPython combines refcounting with a generational cycle detector. __slots__ cuts per-object memory for many small instances; weakref avoids cycles in caches and observers.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which are common causes of memory leaks in a long-running JVM service?

options.text: A static Map used as a cache that never evicts entries.
options.why: Right: static references keep every entry reachable for the life of the class loader.

options.text: ThreadLocal values never removed on pooled threads that live for the whole process.
options.why: Right: pool threads never die, so the values stay reachable; call remove() in finally.

options.text: Listeners or callbacks registered with a long-lived publisher and never deregistered.
options.why: Right: the publisher holds a strong reference to each subscriber.

options.text: Local variables going out of scope when a method returns.
options.why: Stack references vanish on return, so the objects become collectable.

options.text: Choosing G1 instead of the Parallel collector for the old generation.
options.why: Switching collectors changes pause behaviour, not whether reachable objects are retained.

questions.explanation: In a GC language a leak means unintended reachability. Diagnose with a heap dump (jmap or JFR) and find what path from a GC root keeps the objects alive.
